subtopic: ARRANGEMENTS BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES GOVERNING EXTRADITION OF CRIMINALS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ARRANGEMENTS BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES GOVERNING EXTRADITION OF CRIMINALS
speechtext:
A new and comprehensive extradition treaty between Canada and the United States was signed this morning in Washington. The signatories of the treaty were the Canadian minister in the United States, Mr. Leighton McCarthy, for Canada; and Mr. Cordell Hull, the Secretary of State for the United States.
The new treaty, which governs the arrangements between Canada and the United States for the extradition gf criminals who have fled from one country to another, replaces a series of treaties and conventions which began with the Ashburton-Webster treaty 1842, which was subsequently modified by conventions in 1889, 1900, 1905, 1922, and 1925. In 1931 a new treaty, similar to that now signed between Canada and the United States, was entered into between Great Britain and the United States. While the 1931 treaty replaced the Ashburton-Webster treaty and other conventions, it had no effect upon the position of Canada and the United States. Such modifications as have been made in the new treaty are designed to bring the regulations governing extradition into line with modern conditions.
The new treaty is subject to ratification. It will not be published until arrangements have been completed for its presentation to parliament and to the Senate of the United States.

I have been looking into this question and the principle involved. I believe the principle to be this: if the minister will state on his responsibility as a minister that it is not in the public interest to divulge names in answer to an inquiry of this kind, he takes the responsibility and the matter stands there. That of course does not relieve the ministry of the responsibility of giving the information if some other method is adopted of asking for it. As to question No. 3, as I appreciate it the reason might be on an entirely different basis, namely, that these persons who are to be the recipients of subsidies have these subsidies more or less forced on them-I do not understand that they are applicants for subsidies, but by reason of government policy they are entitled to subsidies. Therefore I can understand that it might prejudicially affect their business in the mind of the public. For instance a mortgage company might receive $10,000 for summer-fallowing and carrying on good husbandry. I am not

saying there is such a recipient of government largesse, but there might be, and I think the two things ought to be distinguishable. We ought to be able to work out some satisfactory method which will protect the public interest and at the same time leave to hon. members some of the rights of which I am sorry to think we are being deprived.

I am going to take up this matter as one concerning the privileges of the house. It seems to me that the privileges of the house are being infringed by the refusal of ministers to give information regarding the expenditure of public money. I have been looking up some authorities. I have before me Durell's "Parliamentary Grants". The case that has been made by the opposition for the presentation of accounts of the kind asked for in two of these questions is supported by the practice of the British parliament. I quote from page 2 of Durell:
The bed-rock on which the English system is built is the principle of the maintenance by parliament of control over the grants which it makes. This can only be properly and intelligently discussed if the general principles of the whole system are understood. A preliminary consideration of the English financial system generally is therefore advisable, before dealing with the more restricted subject of control and accounting.
Then it goes on to quote the British practice regarding appropriation and accounting. Again I quote from page 4:
The power of appropriation drew with it the necessity for estimates being regularly laid before the House of Commons, and, by exposing the management of the public revenues, has given the house not only a real and effective control over an essential branch of the executive administration, but in some measure made parliament a partaker in it.
I would like to draw particular attention to these words:
Appropriation alone is, however, of little avail if no provision is made for securing compliance with it. The right of appropriation must be accompanied by the right of parliament to satisfy itself as to the expenditure of the money on the services for which it has been voted.
Then again we have this:
The supreme control of the Commons over public grants, as already mentioned, necessarily demands the complete right of control over the manner in which those grants are spent.
I should like to quote what the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone said in this connection:
It is undoubtedly the business of the House of Commons to be responsible not only for the inception of all public expenditure, but also to follow the money raised by taxation until the last farthing is accounted for.
This authority also deals with the question of withholding information from the house. It
says:

Information in connection with the accounts may be required either for the purpose of testing the accuracy of the accounts-that is to say, for the verification of computation, appropriation, authorities, and regulation; or with a view to investigating the propriety of the expenditure;
or, finally, information may be required not directly connected with the accounts, but relating to the system. Information under the first head cannot be withheld by a department.
In other words it seems to me that the contention that it is the right of this house to demand an accounting of these expenditures "to the uttermost farthing" is perfectly sound and perfectly valid; for we can have no real accounting unless we know where the funds have been spent. I submit we are on sound ground in asking that these questions be answered.

The question before the

A word as to the question of privilege which the hon. leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) has raised. The hon. member has cited from Durell the principles which govern the control by the Commons of all its grants. There can be no question at all as to the Commons having the full right to control all expenditures and the full right to a most complete examination into those expenditures. The point in question is not one of the principle involved; it is a matter of procedure, as to the time, the place and the manner in which control and examination is to be exercised and the possible harm which may result if information is given to parliament in one way rather than in another. The minister has drawn attention to the fact that if the information is presented in one form it might further ulterior purposes which hon. members of the House of Commons would not wish to have served. On the other hand, as my hon. friend knows, in committee of the whole and before other committees and at other times there is ample opportunity to have all the information requested extracted from the ministry if it is desired that this be done.
Of course the rule that governs in these matters equally is that an answer to a question cannot be insisted upon if the answer be refused by the minister on the ground of the public interest. Unquestionably that is why the answer is not being given by the minister at the present time, but that does not mean that at another time, in another place and in another way the Commons may not exercise its full control over the expenditures.

If I may ask a question, I do not understand that either minister has insisted on the ground which the Prime Minister has just mentioned, I believe referring to Beauchesne, which is the same as that appearing in Bourinot. I have not understood that either minister put the refusal on the express ground that it would not be in the public interest to divulge these names. If I may be permitted further-I do not know that I have any right to speak at all-I would say that if the information can be obtained in another way, perhaps in committee of the whole as the Prime Minister suggests or by some other modus operandi, is it not just a farce to say that members cannot obtain it by putting a question on the order paper? There is a principle behind all this, and I am going to ask the ministry to take it into consideration. Is it not in the public interest that we should know where public moneys are going? This matter of answers to questions came up previously in the house, and perhaps it may be as well to clarify and amplify the position as much as possible now.
When the question came up whether a member could withdraw a question and what procedure he should follow, I quoted citation 355 in Beauchesne's "Parliamentary Rules and Forms", which states a ruling made by Mr. Speaker Marcil on January 13, 1910, in which he said:
In my opinion there are only two ways in which a question can be properly withdrawn when once it has been presented for answer in the house, that is, first by written notice by the member putting the question to the clerk of the house, stating that the question is withdrawn, or by the member in his place in the house informing the Speaker that he desired the question to be dropped or withdrawn.
Now we have the question on the order paper; the minister has taken the position that he will give an order for return subject to the deletion of paragraph 4, and the point is whether or not he can be compelled to answer that question. The rule is perfectly clear. The practice here is the same as in England and, as already mentioned by the Prime Minister, citation 353 of Beauchesne states:
An answer to a question cannot be insisted upon, if the answer be refused by the minister on the ground of public interest.
Bourinot, 13th edition, at page 314, states:
An answer to a question cannot be insisted upon, if the answer be refused by a minister on the ground of the public interest, nor can the question be replaced upon the notice paper, nor the refusal of the minister to answer be raised as a question of privilege.
So that there has been no diminution of the powers of hon. members of the house with regard to questions. The practice which is now followed is the practice that has been followed in the past and, as I have already said, the practice which exists in the British House of Commons. When the minister, therefore, on his responsibility takes it upon himself not to answer a question because of the public interest, an answer to the question cannot be insisted upon. There is nothing before the Chair and the Chair is not obliged

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The question as to the advisability of creating an imperial war cabinet has, at different times, been a subject of consideration and consultation between the governments of the several nations of the commonwealth. No formal proposal was made by the government of Great Britain.
The Canadian government expressed the view that the methods of consultation which have come into existence since the last war were more effective as a means of reaching conclusions and decisions as between the several governments of the commonwealth than those afforded by an imperial war cabinet would be. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
1. It is not clear whether the first question refers to the Canadian Red Cross society or to the International Red Cross committee.
The Canadian government have been in frequent touch with the International Red Cross committee at Geneva which have instructed their delegate in Japan to do everything possible to secure information about Canadians, and, whether civilians or combatants, to assist Canadians in Japanese hands. The committee has already transmitted a report on conditions in an internment camp for civilians in Japan and has transmitted some communications concerning Canadians in Japan and Shanghai where the Japanese government is in control.
Up to the present the International Red Cross delegate in Japan has not been able to transmit any- communications to or to receive information about Canadian nationals, whether prisoners of war, interned civilians, or others, in territories such as Hong Kong where the Japanese military authorities are in control.
Both the delegate of the International Red Cross committee and the representative of the protecting power for Canadian interests in Japan have transmitted lists of Canadian nationals interned there. Next of kin of all persons on these lists have been informed and the list was published in the press several weeks ago.
The Canadian Red Cross Society has already provided food parcels for British and Canadian prisoners of war in Germany. Arrangements are being made to extend this service to Hong Kong and also to provide clothing, medical supplies and other necessities for prisoners of war and civilian internees in the Hong Kong area, as soon as it may become possible to send them forward. These arrangements involve correspondence between the various governments and National Red Cross Societies concerned, and negotiations through the protecting power and International Red Cross committee. As they have not yet been completed, it is not thought advisable that information about them should be made public at this stage.
2. So far as is known there are no Canadian prisoners of war in Japan. There appear to be about 70 Canadian civilians interned there but they are not classed as prisoners of war. Information so far received appears to indicate that the interned civilians are being employed only on work in connection with the maintenance of the camps. No official reports have been received about Canadian prisoners of war in Hong Kong. The Minister of National Defence has given to parliament statistics of the members of the Canadian forces who were in Hong Kong before the Japanese invasion and of a report which had been received on the number of casualties. Information received from diverse scources appears to indicate that there are about 2,000 Canadians including members of the armed forces and civilians interned in Hong Kong and Kowloon by the Japanese. It does not appear that any of the Canadians detained by the Japanese in	Hong Kong and
Kowloon are being employed by the Japanese although it may be assumed that they are doing work about their camps. No definite information is available on medical services and hospitalization, although reports received from various sources would indicate that medical services and hospitalization are inadequate. No information is available from official sources on food rations being supplied but information from China which has reached the government indicates that the food situation is unsatisfactory, the staple diet provided the prisoners being soup and rice. It is reported that some additional food supplies can be purchased by prisoners and internees but no information as to the amounts or kinds is as yet available.

That a select committee be appointed to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent . with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein, and that notwithstanding standing order 65 the committee shall consist of twenty-four members, as follows: Messrs. Abbott, Bercovitch, Black (Cumberland), Boucher, Bradette, Chevrier, Cleaver, Douglas (Weyburn), Fournier (Hull), Gladstone, Golding, Graham, Harris (Danforth), Homuth, Johnston (Bow River), Macdonald (Halifax), Mayhew, Mcllraith, Picard, Pottier, Reid, Ross (Moose Jaw), Sissons, Winkler, with power to send for persons, papers and records; to examine witnesses and to report from time to time to the house.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, this resolution is
identical with the one which I moved a year ago, and is similar in all particulars to the resolution with respect to war expenditures which was adopted at Westminster, and which has been the basis of any inquiries which have been made with regard to war expenditures in Great Britain. The only change in this resolution from the previous one is that the name of Mr. Boucher is substituted for that of Mr. Diefenbaker, and that of Mr. Homuth for Mr. Green, and Mr. Winkler for Mr. Thorson.
The committee appointed last year made several reports to the house during the last session. At one time I thought of including in this resolution some of the additional powers which were given to last year's committee in accordance with its requests from time to time, but upon reflection it seemed preferable to introduce the resolution exactly as it was introduced a year ago. No doubt the committee at its first meeting will ask the house to renew the additional powers given to it last year.
When I introduced the original resolution I made a comprehensive survey of British procedure, cited numerous British precedents, and generally sought to give to the house an expression of the British attitude in dealing with this all-important matter of public expenditures relating to the war. I do not intend to-day to repeat what I said at that time. There is no necessity for doing so, because it appears on Hansard.
I should like on behalf of the government to take this opportunity to thank members of all parties who served on the committee last year for the sustained and devoted labour given piece-meal without doing a great deal

I have no doubt that the members who are to be on the committee this year will find through membership on the committee as did the members last year an opportunity for service of the highest character to the country at this particular time.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt that the members of the war expenditures committee will have a very ungrateful task before them. Its work will be tremendous if the committee goes into all expenditures by war departments.
There is one thing I do not understand. It is that the public accounts committee has been nominated each year for the last eleven years, and yet has not sat in all that time. I do not see the use of appointing a public accounts committee that does not sit. I would point out that during the last war in particular all these matters of war expenditures were studied by the public accounts committee, and its reports were made public.
If we are to follow the Westminster practice, I do not see why we should not have a committee on national economy to study items of expenditure in the war departments as well as in the others. There is a great difference between our new system and that at Westminster and also the system in the United States congress. At Westminster they have complete public accounts, and at Washington the estimates, which they call the budget, are given in a book as large as the telephone directory of the city of New York. Here we give much simpler information, and I wonder whether the public accounts com-miteee will be called to do something with regard to public expenditures.

cow beef for the beef specified in the contract, but in the belief that if the committee is going to deal with the idea of Canada going into an all-out war effort, we must realize that there are a great many industries in the country which to-day are producing nothing in the way of war materials. They are not producing these materials because in the early part of the war the government paid for the tooling up of certain industries to produce certain commodities which we needed. Today we let our contracts by tender, and we do so because we think it is the proper thing to do. The industries that were tooled up are able now to underbid industries that never made any of those products, with the result that the industries originally making these products are crowded with orders and it is impossible to produce the amount they ought to turn out, whereas a good many nonessential industries which to-day ought to be doing the same thing are not doing it because the government or the departments-and I find no fault-feel that it would be wrong for them not to ask for tenders, and that they must accept the lowest tenders. I suggest that in view of the vote on Monday, in view of the fact that to-day we are engaged in an all-out war effort, we must make up our minds. It is not a question of the cost of one or two cents on a unit that costs $2.50 or $4 or $5. It is a question of putting all the effort of our man-power and every machine into the war work in which we are engaged. I am one of those who are not prepared to find fault with the government if they say to industry, "It is going to cost a little more to produce things in your industry than the cost of the lowest tender, but we have to get the goods we need."
Our idea in studying these matters in the committee is not that of trying to uncover scandal or some things that might hurt the government, because I am not interested in that, much as I should like to see them out of office. I am concerned with the war effort, and I feel that the committee could do better work-I am not saying this to belittle what was done in the past-by trying to work with the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and other ministers of the government in an endeavour to put the whole industrial force of the country behind the war effort, instead of going ahead as we are doing today, perhaps giving some industries far more business than they can handle, while other industries which are more or less non-essential are not doing any job for the war. It is with that proviso that I accept the responsibility as a member of this committee.

As a member of last year's committee during the latter part of the year, I think that in spite of the limitations under which they laboured they did a good job. In the fields which they examined they went into the matter quite thoroughly and, I think, presented to this house something of a comprehensive report on the subjects into which they had inquired. In that regard, I say, they did a good job. But I rise primarily in order to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to interpret to the house the order of reference in this particular resolution.
Last year, I remember, there was some discussion as to what the powers of the committee really were, and it was contended that we were to inquire into defence services and to report what, if any, economies, consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government, might be effected therein and that, therefore, we were limited in certain respects by the order of reference. It seems to me that if this committee is going to be useful this year, it should go into the much wider and more important field of the department which is providing the supplies for the defence departments. I refer particularly to the Department of Munitions and Supply.
If this order of reference is sufficient to enable the committee to deal adequately with all matters which they may wish to examine in connection with the operations of the Department of Munitions and Supply, then I am satisfied with the order; if on the other hand the committee is to be narrowed down to the recommendation of economies which may be effected in relation to the three defence services, then I contend that this committee is not going to do the job which really must be done this year. I feel that we have reached the stage in Canada, where, without endeavouring only to uncover scandals dr anything of that sort, we ought to look into the operations of the department which is making large expenditures in relation to the provision of supplies for the army, the navy, the air force and in other fields.
I am-and I state it quite frankly-alarmed at the state of things in this country. Since the war broke out we have seen powerful industrialists, and those who serve powerful industrialists and monopolies, placed in key positions in connection with the purchase of supplies and the control of the economic side of our war effort. I do not believe that is wise or good. I do not believe it is wise, because it undermines the confidence of the great masses of the people in what is being done in this country. I have heard it stated over and over again by people of quite moderate views,

War Expenditures-Mr. Coldwell
not extremists by any means, that when they look at the names of the people who surround the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) they wonder whether the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and all their friends are not assembled in that department. I think I said in the house during the debate on the address that in my opinion this was dangerous to the country; that if our war effort is to be properly and effectively controlled in a manner that will command and retain the confidence of the Canadian people, then much wider representation should be given in the control of these economic organizations. I am thoroughly of opinion that this war expenditures committee this year-without any reflection whatsoever on the minister or those employed in the department-ought thoroughly to investigate the operations of that department. I think it is our obligation to do this.
I quoted a little while ago from Durell's "Parliamentary Grants," and one of the most interesting sections in that authoritative volume deals with grants made by parliament in wartime. It deals with the experiences of the British in the South African war, and deals particularly with their experiences during the great war. The book itself is dedicated to the Right Hon. David Lloyd George, and much of it was written during the last great war. It points out that it is the duty of the civil authority to examine very carefully all expenditures made in connection with the operation of war. It says, and rightly, that war is an extravagant business, a wasteful business, even if it is a necessary business; that during wartime the normal peace controls must be removed; that decisions have to be made quickly, some of them involving perhaps certain expenditures which are necessary but which turn out later on to be extravagances; that it is more essential in wartime than in peacetime that every detail of public expenditure should be thoroughly scrutinized.
I have been following with some degree of interest the work of the committee in the United States. I do not know what the condition is in our own country in regard to the power of some of these great organizations which are so well represented in the Department of Munitions and Supply. But I have read of the attitude of the Standard Oil company, of the situation created by the steel corporation, the aluminum company, the great corporations of the United States and so forth. I think it is the duty of this House of Commons to make sure that nothing of that kind has happened or is happening here. That ought to be one of the duties of a committee fMr. Coldwell.]
of this kind. Its scope should not be narrowed down as some of us understood it was last year.

There was no restriction
whatsoever upon the scope of the committee's work.

I would say to the minister, who was chairman of the committee last year, that quite often it was said it was not the business of our sub-committee to go into the Department of Munitions and Supply and particular contracts.

There was an inquiry into the Department of Munitions and Supply, and it was indicated later on that there would be the fullest opportunity of making any inquiry that the committee might wish to make into the operations of that department. There was no restriction last year; there will be no restriction this year.

I am glad to know there will be no restriction this year. I know of no investigation being made into that department last year, although I think the members of the committee were all agreed that when the committee sat again that should be its principal job. I am urging that if there is any doubt as to the meaning of this order of reference it should be clarified, so that we may have a clear understanding that the committee this year may devote the major portion of its time to a study of the Department of Munitions and Supply.
The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) raised the question of the public accounts committee. That is a peace-time organization. That committee should be sitting all the time to examine our normal peacetime expenditures. The committee which it is now proposed to set up is a special war committee to examine expenditures in connection with the war. Of course I recognize immediately that there are certain questions regarding the provision of supplies for the army, such, for example, as the number of guns, number of tanks, number of aeroplanes, the places where they are, the cost of them and so on, that, if answered openly in this house, might give information of value to the enemy. But it seems to me that there is no reason in the world why a committee of this house should not go quite thoroughly into the matter of expenditures for the provision of equipment.
I am therefore in support of this resolution. But I urge that this year there shall be no doubt as to what the committee is going to do -I will put it that way-that instead of dividing the committee into three subcommittees to look into three parts of the war services,

War Expenditures-Mr. Hansell
the committee make it its main business, its entire business if you will, this session, to look into the expenditures and operations of the Department of Munitions and Supply and the contracts that hon. members would wish to examine that have been and are being let by that department. At the same time I suggest that the committee think over carefully the large expenditures that have been made by this government and with the British government in their establishment of government-owned industries in this country, so that we may understand how they are controlled and what the implications of those controls may be for the future; for there is vividly in my mind a recollection of a suggestion made that even during the process of this war a committee of business men might examine those organizations and might recommend how they shall be salvaged when the war ends. I think it is the duty of this parliament to see, not how these new industries and new plants can be salvaged after the war but how they may be utilized for the good of the Canadian people when the time comes; and that meantime this country should be protected against those who consciously or unconsciously on account of their economic interests are anxious to see that their interests rather than the interests of the great masses of the people of this country are protected.

In rising to speak to this motion, having been a member of the committee that sat last year I should like to make a few remarks and perhaps a few suggestions for the consideration of hon. members who will comprise the committee this coming year.
I must say I was a little surprised at the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) with respect to restrictions on the work of this committee. I well remember my first experience with this committee, when I asked definitely as to the scope of its work. I recognized that all war expenditures were not mentioned in the little stereotyped programme that was handed to us, and I asked the chairman of the committee, the present Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson), whether or not we had a right to investigate all war expenditures. I used this illustration: "I do not notice ships mentioned in this little programme. Have we the right to investigate the money that has been spent in the construction of ships?" The minister replied, "Yes, we have the right to go into any war expenditures."
Even at that, the point is not that we do not have the right to go into any sort of war expenditures whatever. The point is that
we do not have time to go into these matters. For instance, this committee has not met,
I think, during the last nine months. It was not set up until late in the session; after the session was concluded it adjourned for a couple of weeks, then came back and sat for five or perhaps six weeks. Then it adjourned again and nothing has been done until now. As a result, though the committee was divided into three subcommittees, I am sure all those who served on the committee will agree that we only began to touch the mere fringe of war expenditures in this country. The subcommittee on which I served had the opportunity to investigate expenditures in respect to the medical services of the various branches of the Department of National Defence. Well, I am sure we only touched the fringe of that, subject. We had the right to investigate expenditures in relation to salvage. We did not even get into that question. We had the right to investigate expenditures in respect to gasoline and oil, but we did not even get into that matter. If this committee is to be of any value at all to this house and the country, if it is to accomplish that which it should be designed to accomplish, it will have to work hard and long, and will have to remain in session almost three hundred and sixty-five days in the year.
In dealing with the work of this committee, Mr. Speaker, and also with the work of the committee that is about to be set up, I wish to say a word in respect to secret sessions, or sessions held in camera. It seems to me that this sort of thing is becoming more or less a joke. We speak of sitting behind closed doors, but we might just as well throw the doors wide open and let the public in. If we have any objection to letting the public in, however, I suggest that we might just as well let the press in. I am sure the representatives of the press would play ball with us. If there should1 be a little bit of evidence of such a nature that we could not possibly let it go out, I am confident those men would say, "All right; that is off the record, and we will not print it". Some of us regarded these sessions as being secret, only to find after a few days, a few weeks or a month or two that information coming from some source appeared in the newspapers and periodicals of this country in bold type. I have here a clipping which I took from a newspaper. You cannot read it, Mr. Speaker, but you can see that it includes several columns, and it contains a report of the work of this committee. I do not know how that got out, when the committee was supposed to be sitting behind closed doors. I might mention another occasion, when none

War Expenditures-Mr. Hansell
other than Air Commodore R. W. Ryan, who was director of the Royal Canadian Air Force medical services, was on the stand. That afternoon the press were excluded, and I recall that Air Commodore Ryan said, "Now, I am giving you something that is absolutely confidential". I need not mention what it was, but we regarded it as confidential and treated it as such. The committee concluded its work in August, I believe, and on November 25 there appeared in the press a report almost a column in length, dealing with that afternoon session. Someone must have had access to the records. They must have gone to the office where the records were kept, taken out the records, looked them over and reported upon them.
I have no particular objection to these matters being reported. My point is simply that if a session is regarded as secret by all of us, then somebody somewhere is breaking confidence. I might mention as a further illustration another committee which sat about a year ago. A secret document was brought before the committee by an officer from the Department of Justice. He would not even let that document out of his hands. He would not permit it to be passed around. It was something that he had received from a foreign legation here. But what happened? We regarded it as secret, but not long afterward a certain member of this house read that secret document over a national radio hook-up in Canada. When I placed questions about that incident on the order paper last session the hon. member who read the document thought I was finding fault with him. I was not. The fault did not lie with the hon. member. I suppose most of us, if we could get access to something of that kind and broadcast it over a national hook-up, might do the same thing; in fact I do not think we would lose any time in doing so. But I place the responsibility for that occurrence upon the Department of Justice, whose representative considered the document to be secret and would not even let the committee see it. Then it was given to one of the members of this house, on the government side, to read over the radio.
I say that at that time the government, through the Department of Justice, broke faith with the work of the committee. I put a question on the order paper asking if any other hon. member would have the same opportunity of having access to such documents and reading them over the air. The answer was that that was a matter of government policy. The only conclusion one can make with respect to an answer of the land is that the govern-
ment policy is to let one of the Liberal members read it, but not to let any member of the opposition read it. That is the only conclusion one can come to.
Now, to get down to the work of this committee, last year we investigated some of the medical services of the army and the air force. May I say in passing that this is the only opportunity we have had in a year to discuss the work of that committee. It has reported several times-I do not know how many. There has been no motion for concurrence in any of the reports, and while we have been able to discuss war expenditures in the various branches of the service, through the defence ministers, in committee of the whole, we have not been able to carry on a discussion on the basis of the work of the war expenditures committee.
To me at least it was a glaring fact that there was not sufficient coordination between the army, the navy, the air force and the Department of Pensions and National Health with respect to the medical services of these branches of the forces. Perhaps my language would not be considered vulgar if I were to say that each seemed desirous of running its own little show. It did seem to me that there was an element of that principle, all through the evidence. While the suggestion may not be acceptable to the Minister of National Defence and to the other defence ministers, my own observations lead me to suggest that there should be one department or, shall I say, one great organization for the conduct of the medical services of all, and that this organization should be under the Department of Pensions and National Health. I know that the suggestion will not be acceptable, but to my mind there is no good argument against it. It was the view of one of the outstanding medical witnesses who gave evidence to the committee. I see no reason why it could not be carried out, and it would effect the saving of a great deal of money.
The Department of Pensions and National Health purchases its own supplies, while the Department of Munitions and Supply purchases the medical supplies, for the rest of the forces. It seems logical that if a man has appendicitis it makes no difference whether he wears the uniform of the air force, the army or the navy; he has appendicitis just the same. If a man has a fractured leg, it does not matter whether he is in one branch of the service or the other. Not only could there be greater coordination, but in my view if the medical services of the country were under one department and one head they could be carried on more efficiently.

War Expenditures-Mr. Hansell
The evidence before the committee showed that the Department of Pensions and National Health had a good deal of bed space to spare, while some of the other branches of the forces were overcrowded. I recall that the committee took one trip to Toronto and while there visited a small hospital which in peace-time was known as Grace hospital, situated at the corner of two busy streets. It had been abandoned by the hospital authorities of Toronto as being inadequate for hospital purposes. When we went in there it seemed to be full of patients. The corridors were narrow and the equipment was anything but what it should have been That hospital came under the medical services of the army. From there we went to the magnificently equipped Christie street hospital, operated by the Department of Pensions and National Health. There we found about 800 beds available. I believe that condition could be duplicated right across Canada. I can see no reason why the medical branches of the three armed services could not be coordinated with the medical services under the Department of Pensions and National Health. I know the present rule states that no man may come under the Department of Pensions and National Health until he reaches category E or is discharged. Well, a rule can easily be altered. After all, it is only a rule, and one of the functions of governmental administration is the altering of rules. The government has altered plenty of rules in the past few years, and there is no reason why a change could not be made in this instance.
I have something further to say which may not be strictly in line with the idea of economizing in war expenditures. Each war service controls its own medical branch and has its own hospitals. Each air-training school, for instance, has hospital accommodation, either small or large. May I make a suggestion to the government which, I believe, would coincide with what was said a little while ago by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, in connection with the salvage of this equipment after the war. I suggest that wherever possible, instead of building hospitals in air training schools and military camps they should build additional permanent space in the civil hospitals, and equip those hospitals for the added responsibilities they will have to shoulder. If this were done, when the war ends the communities concerned would have assets. There can be no question that there are hundreds of communities in Canada which lack proper hospital facilities.
There is a number of air training schools in my constituency. The government has
been very liberal with me; I believe there are more in my constituency than in the constituency of any other member of parliament.
You must have some good will.

I have ways. A number of these air training schools are situated within a few miles of town. For instance, take the town of Macleod-I am sure the picture will be the same in other constituencies -with a population of nearly 2,000 people and a hospital of twenty-five beds. There is a huge air training school just across the tracks, right on the edge of town, and this school has its own little hospital. Why could not the amount of money spent on that hospital, or a little more if you please, have been put into an addition to the hospital already located in the town, making it a permanent feature that could service the air training school and yet be an asset to the community when the war is over? I think that is worth considering.
I do not believe I shall be breaking any of the rules if I read part of the evidence that was given to the committee, because it was not in any sense confidential. We had the evidence of a man who was an authority on hospitalization. I asked him:
What would be your attitude to a suggestion that an addition be built to that hospital at the hospital's expense but the government underwriting that additional expense for so many years; guaranteeing the loan, and so forth- underwriting it-so that the hospital could care for the army or air force patients in those districts and when the war is over still have the accommodation for their civilian purposes?
This is the answer:
Yes. I foresee at the end, if this war goes five years or four years even, if there is no building of civilian hospitals at the end of this war we are going to be very short of accommodation if these people are going to be thrown back on the civilian institutions; and that was one of the purposes of my letter to the Prime Minister, to try to get something that would cushion the shock of the change-over.
I do not think I need to read all this. The argument is used that the air force must have a hospital at its quarters in case of crashes, but the reply would be that crashes do not always take place over the airport. They may occur thirty, forty or fifty miles away, and the men involved are rushed to the nearest hospital. I make that as a suggestion, and I ask the government to give it serious consideration.
There is another point I should like to raise in connection with the work of the committee that will sit this year. It will experience the same difficulty in extracting evi-

War Expenditures-Mr. Hansell
dence from those who are in the different services, in the army, the air force and the navy, as was experienced by the committee that sat last year. The members are going to find it difficult because of the military attitude that is to be found throughout the services. An officer in the army appears and attempts to give evidence, but when he finds that he does not agree with his superior officers, I challenge the committee to get evidence out of that man.
Not if it is in open session.
It is not only in the closed sessions that that occurs.
Oh, yes.

My hon. friend says, "oh yes," but I should like to read some of the evidence. I will not give the name of the man who was on the stand, but there was nothing private about this matter because no information was revealed. When we found that we could not get any information, the chairman asked this question:
You notice the point we are concerned with -the duplication of agencies. Have you thought about that at all-how to eliminate and still perform the task-how to eliminate the unnecessary duplication?
The answer is:
I think that is a question for the senior men in charge of the services to decide among themselves; it is not for me to pass any opinion on anybody else; it is their duty, it is their prerogative, shall we say.
I am not blaming that man for adopting that attitude; I suppose he could not help it. Another question follows by the chairman:
We are in camera, and it is our duty as members of parliament-
A. And I am in the army.
Q. Mr. Picard: But we are here as a committee to investigate some aspects of army administration.
A. Sure.
Q. The Chairman: We represent the taxpayers and you are one of them.
A. Very much so.
Q. And we would like to draw on your wide experience. Have you any thought on that?
A. No. I do not think it is right to ask me.
I am convinced that that gentleman had the facts. I am convinced also that he was a witness who knew whereof he spoke, yet because he realized that he disagreed with his superior officer he dared not venture the evidence. That is the position in which the committee found itself on that occasion. I am not a lawyer; perhaps some hon. members of the committee who were lawyers could have extracted the evidence. I understand that the chairman is a lawyer, and there were a few

others, but they could not get it. It may be necessary sometimes to go outside the services altogether in order to get evidence, or there may have to be some principle brought into play under which these men will be completely protected.
Another matter to which there has been little reference is that of patents and inventions. Quite often we read a news item stating that some man has invented something that may prove useful to our war services. Eor instance, a few years ago a carburettor was supposed to be invented by some gentleman that would run a car a hundred miles or some very large mileage on a gallon of gasoline. There was a good deal of reference to it in the press.
The Pogue carburettor.

I do not know whether
it was Pogue or Poke; anyway it never came into general use. Perhaps the Minister of Munitions and Supply or some other expert will tell us that it never did exist, but there is a feeling throughout this country that the inventive genius which may be inherent in Canada can sometimes be sabotaged by the big interests if it happens to interfere with their private profits. I do not know whether that is true or not, but I do know that in the United States of America the government has set up what is known as a national inventors' council under their Department of Trade and Commerce. That council will receive any invention that anyone under heaven cares to send them. All the ramifications of copyrights and all that are avoided, so that even if a young high school lad has discovered some little twist or something of that kind to improve something, he can send it direct to the council. All these suggestions are looked over by the council and if there is any merit whatsoever in any idea submitted, it is passed on by the council to their research board, by whatever name it may be called, and is tested. If the test proves that the invention is worth while it is passed on to the army, navy or air force or whatever branch may be involved, and the person who first suggested the idea is given adequate compensation for his discovery. Something like that should be done in Canada. I believe it would be a tremendous encouragement and of great benefit.
There is another point about it. We know that inventions, royalties, copyright and all that sort of thing constitute a tremendously complicated question. Anyone in this country or any institution in this country which would take any such invention and sabotage it in the interests of their own profits is performing an act of treachery, if that is not too strong

War Expenditures-Mr. McCann
a word. They are saboteurs indeed. This is something that is well within the realm of possibility because the other day I saw by the press that a committee of the United States senate was investigating this sort of thing. The clipping which I have here says:
Among other things the committee was told of a vast patent pool linking the General Electric company with Krupp interests in Germany which prevented greater manufacture of cemented tungsten carbide. [DOT]
Another cartel agreement between German interests and the Remington Arms company had at one time impeded American sales of military ammunition to Britain and other parts of the empire.
I do not know what goes on behind the scenes at the Department of the Secretary of State, who has copyright and inventions under his administration; but I am quite certain that all the inventive genius which there is in this country and which could have been utilized should be brought into play and be used in the prosecution of this war. If there is a carburettor anywhere in this country that will save only one mile a gallon on gas we should know it, and if that idea has been sabotaged the saboteurs should be dealt with accordingly.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
I have not much time left.
Has he not seen in the evidence that an expert made the statement before one of the subcommittees in the United States that the Pogue carburettor was impracticable?

That is
not borne out by what Mr. Pogue said himself. I have corresponded with him.

Answering my hon. friend's question, I do recall evidence given to that effect, but I also recall that when that gentleman gave that evidence he said, "Hush now, boys, this is not to go on the record," and that is why I did not. mention it this afternoon. My hon. friend has mentioned it; I have not. The gentleman said that that carburettor was so much boloney. I do not know whether he had seen it or not. Maybe it is so much boloney, but this country was given to understand that it was not, and that such a carburettor was in existence. I am not finding fault with the work of the committee. I am simply making the suggestion that the government set up a council on inventions, to which a man can bring his ideas or discoveries or inventions, without having to go through all the various ramifications
of the copyright office, for which procedure he requires a lot of money, and many a poor inventor has no money.
Why waste time when there is an inventions board now?

If there is a national
inventions council in Canada I have not heard about it. That may be my fault, but if I have not heard about it, and I am here for five or six months of the year, I conclude that the rest of the country knows nothing about it. In the United States the work of their inventions council is publicized. They say in effect:	"Come on, you Americans;
if you have any suggestions to make, make them to us." Certainly that is not being done in Canada, even though an inventions board may be in existence here.
May I say in conclusion that I am, of course, in harmony with the government and with the committee in desiring to reduce, so far as practicable, war expenditures. If, however, we attempt to reduce war expenditures in this country at the expense of efficiency, we shall be making a huge mistake. We have found- and I know the committee will agree with me -that some departments needed more money than they were able to lay their hands on for particular purposes. We went down to the hospital at Petawawa and were taken through the nurses' quarters.
Oh I

My hon. friend does not
like to think that we were taken through the nurses' quarters. We saw the nurses sitting on nail kegs because they had no chairs in their rooms. What they needed there was a little more money, instead of a little less. The brigadier who was showing us around said, "You ask us to cut down our expenditures. I wonder what we could cut out here." There was not very much they could cut out in those quarters.

The hon. member's time
has expired.

If I may, Mr. Speaker, I shall take not more than half a minute to conclude.
The Social Credit philosophy is simply this: if a thing is physically possible, let us make the treasury reflect that fact. Let us save in every possible way every material thing we possess, but do not let us impair our efficiency by paring down expenditures where that does not seem to be absolutely necessary.

The brief observations I have to make have to

War Expenditures-Mr. McCann
do more with the motion before the house at the present time than with the discussion of the report of the war expenditures committee of last year. In passing, however, may I say I agree with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) in several of the remarks which he has made. As a matter of fact, I appeared as a witness before the war expenditures committee last year, and several of the recommendations which I made are recommendations which the member for Macleod is making to-day. I am very glad to tell him that some of those recommendations made by myself a year ago are being acted upon. For instance, with reference to hospitalization, grants have been made to civilian hospitals in different parts of the country with a view to augmenting and extending their facilities to be used in wartime purposes for our armed forces, and they may in later years be used for the civil population.
In looking over the personnel of the present committee I observe that geographical considerations appear to be given more prominence than either the capability or the experience of those on the committee to hold the type of investigation that will come before them. In a committee consisting of twenty-four members, there are fourteen lawyers. Fortunately, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has seen fit to put along with them one or two preachers to guide them along the right path. Last year there was quite an investigation with reference to hospitalization and medical and1 dental services. The heads of the dental services of the three branches of the armed forces appeared before the committee.
A very considerable amount of money has been expended in connection with hospitalization. Much more will be expended in other years, and enormous quantities of supplies are being bought for the three branches of the service. It will be noted, however, that on the committee that is appointed there is not a single medical man, although there are fifteen or twenty medical men in the house. In. the matter of selection that is an oversight. If we want to use the capabilities and facilities which are at hand in this house, then they should be put in the places where they can be of best service, and I submit to the Prime Minister, or whoever is responsible for this and similar committees, that there are in the house engineers, dentists, doctors, and other men, especially medical men, who could give valuable service on committees with reference to hospitalization, expenditures 
on construction, expenditures on medical and dental supplies. Yet their services are not used.
I laugh when I read the personnel of the committee, and I laugh at myself when I am put on the fisheries committee, when I do not know any more about lobsters or the fishing industry than other hon. gentlemen know about medicine. If such a situation applies to myself, I do not doubt that on analysis it will be found to apply to a great many others. I suggest to the Prime Minister, therefore, that in the setting up of the committee they utilize the services of some medical men who could give them valuable information as a result of their lifelong experience in the medical field, and the same thing applies to dentists with regard to the matter of dental services. Valuable assistance could be obtained from the experience of these men.

I want to take a few moments to lodge a vigorous protest against the manner in which parliament has been compelled to conduct the nation's business, particularly during the war. I am sure that every person who cherishes democratic institutions to-day must be concerned with regard to the fact that parliamentary institutions in this country have to some extent fallen into disrepute. One has only to read the daily press and some of the popular periodicals and listen to conversations in railway smoking cars and on the street to realize that parliament has become fair game for punsters, wits and columnists. While it is true that some of the criticism is not fair or justified, it must also be said that we ourselves in this house must accept some share of responsibility for the fact that there is a growing feeling that parliament has become largely a talk-shop rather than a workshop.
Hear, hear.
The "hear, hear" does not affect me. I have taken very little time in this house in the past few weeks, but I assume that hon. members approve what I say.
You are right, whether you take time or not.
