speechtext: May I ask the hon. member what is the date of that report?
It was tabled in the British House of Commons on May 28, 1940.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That was the
very reference I quoted last year as an example of the kind of thing our committee might be expected to do.

If that is a
good example I should think the Prime Minister would have had this committee appointed about January 28, rather than April 29. I have a number of reports here. I need not bother to quote them all, but I would refer to one which refers to propaganda in Great Britain. Many of us have been critical of the type of British propaganda that has been carried on, and it is rather interesting to see what the committee has to say about the films issued by the British ministry:
Against the three films which the ministry was able to influence and assist must be set a number of cases in which commercial producers made films -which they thought were excellent propaganda but which in the opinion of the ministry were disastrous and were calculated to have precisely the effect which the minister did not desire. This state of affairs would be ludicrous if it were not intolerable. It has arisen through the lack of sufficiently close cooperation and mutual understanding between the industry and the ministry, the need for which has already been emphasized. Day-to-day interference by the minister in the affairs of commercial producers is to be deprecated.
I need not quote the many other reports I have; hon. members can obtain them from the parliamentary library, but I do invite hon. gentlemen to give them some consideration. In England they have made use of practically every private member of the house,

War Expenditures-Mr. Church
working on subcommittees. At a time like this, when the tentacles of government have reached into almost every aspect of our economy, for its own sake and for the sake of the morale of the Canadian people, as well as for the reputation of parliament, the government should have every aspect of its activity constantly subjected to the scrutiny and examination of members of this house. I feel that the government would do well to make use of hon. members in this way. The Prime Minister has sitting behind him a great many private members who have had experience in various walks of life and who are given very little opportunity to do any work of the sort being done in England. I feel that it would be of tremendous help not only to them but to Canada as well if subcommittees of this type were set up. Now, almost three months after parliament was convened, we are setting up a small committee of twenty-four members, broken up into three subcommittees of eight members. They cannot begin to do the work that should be done. There is no reason why a dozen subcommittees should not be set up dealing with the various aspects of Canada's war effort. There is no reason why hon. members could not be grouped, not necessarily by provinces or by parties, but according to their particular training and experience. I feel that they would greatly assist the ministers; that through these committees the ministers would get advice based on the experience of the members, instead of having, as we have had for the last two or three days, members rise in committee of the whole and present individual cases to one minister or another. We cannot conduct the business of a nation in that way. If every hon. member of this house were to bring from his files all the individual cases which have come to his attention and place them before the Minister of National Defence, that minister alone would be here for six months. But if we had committees to go over these cases, they could come to some conclusions with respect to them; they could make suggestions as to changes in policy; they could offer recommendations to the ministers, and many of the cases of hardship or injustice or miscarriage of administration would never come into this house at all. Then this parliament would become what it should be, a place for the discussion of policies, and matters of administration could be dealt with by a large number of committees made up of private members of this house.
I do not offer this suggestion merely because I want to see private members have more to do, or merely because I want to find some new opportunity to criticize the government.
I offer these suggestions to the government because I am convinced that if we are to win this war we must maintain the morale of the Canadian people. We are constantly repeating in public statements that this is a war for democracy, but we have [DOT] to convince the people that democracy is a reality; that it is not some outworn shibboleth that belongs to the nineteenth century but is something which can operate in our day; that it can operate more efficiently and more effectively than the totalitarian states can operate; that it can harness the experience and ability of private members representing the people, and use that experience and ability in the common task of winning the war. I feel certain that if we do this the position of parliament will be much enhanced in the mind of the Canadian people, and the government will be greatly assisted.

Mr. Speaker, if this resolution passes to-day, in my opinion parliamentary government will be at an end in Canada. Over a hundred years ago they had a civil war in England in order to obtain control over the executive and of all expenditures. Since this war started this parliament has had no such control over anything. Here the session is almost two-thirds gone

this is the fifty-third day of it- and the government bring in a motion at this late hour to appoint a committee, to do what? To take out of the hands of this parliament any remaining control it may have over the expenditures in connection with the war or discussion of it from now on. So far, that control has been very little and is a myth. We have rules and regulations of the house; we have statutes; we have the auditor general and an audit act; we have a treasury board, which is supposed to pass on estimates, allotments and commitments and guard the treasury. We are simply going around as a parliament in a circle because control is daily taken from us. For many years I was a member of the public accounts committee, but since the Bren gun matter in April, 1939, I doubt if that committee has had a meeting; at least I do not remember one.
To-day with these rising billions of dollars in uncontrolled estimates, the people are wondering what kind of parliament this is when we allow money in astronomical figures to be spent like water by the government absolutely without any control or authority on the part of this parliament or its knowing a thing about it. What audit is made of the nearly $4,000,000 a day which is being expended on the war by the various departments of government and all these outside boards and commissions? I raised that ques-

War Expenditures-Mr. Church
tion last year in connection with the estimates of the Minister of Finance. I asked: Does the auditor general audit each account in detail, and, if not, what check or audit is provided by law, statute, custom or usage, and by whom? Here we are at the fifty-third day of this session, and at this stage we are asked to pass this resolution by which we consent to hand over to a select committee all these billions without any check or control or say in it, over our heads.
What is the object of appointing this select committee? Speaking on the appointment of a similar select committee on war expenditures last year, as reported at page 1257 of Hansard for March 5, 1941, I said:
What is the object of having a select committee if it is going to have its hands tied behind its back through the failure of the government to give it the power which any committee should have ill order to function properly regarding war expenditures, manpower, recruiting, munitions and overseas policies. . . .
I notice by the explanation which the Prime Minister gave of the resolution last night that the committee has no power to go into any question of government policy.
If it has no power to do that, why is the committee appointed?
As far as this war is concerned the committee will have its bands tied behind its back because it has no power to deal with any question of government policy regarding the war. .	.	.
My second point is this: the government has decided that it is to be the tutor, custodian and guardian of the committee. The committee is not to be allowed to do anything but what the government allows it to do. The government will decide, so far as its war effort is concerned what information shall be kept secret and what not. No member of this house wants to give the enemy any information-
But I say this, that at the present time Canada needs an auditor general like the late Auditor General McDougall. Auditor General McDougall, thou should'st be living now! Canada hath need of thee, right at this very hour-as Wordsworth said of Milton-because "never were there as many who knew so little about so much." History will condemn this House of Commons for having allowed all these expenditures without the power to deal with this matter in the manner indicated.
I am dealing only with the system and great principle of parliamentary control. The men nominated to the committee are all good men. They have done admirable work. I have sat on committees with some of them, and they are some of the best men in the House of Commons. It will be understood, therefore that I am not saying anything about the personnel of the committee, but the system functions and policy herein. When

the committee has its hands tied behind its back, and is refused power to function, when secret meetings are held and we have reports made thereof to parliament and no concurrence in the findings; when we have an estimate made by the treasury board of $1,325,000 for war expenditure and have a deficit of over $135,000,000 at the end of the fiscal year and when we get up in the clouds this way, then I say it is high time parliament had some control over war expenditures, because the minister can himself authorize them when the treasury board is not meeting.
The figure for the next year's expenditures is set at S2,200,000,000.	What control has
parliament over those expenditures? It has no control whatsoever. I am not a believer in this lack of any system. We know that in the mother of parliaments there is a war expenditures committee. But that committee sits nearly three hundred days in the year. It sits when the house is in session. On the other hand, the committee in this parliament, has not, up to this fifty-third day of the session, held a single meeting. It is not yet appointed. Neither has the public accounts committee sat.
As I said last year with regard to these particular matters:
I have already expressed the hope in this house that this committee will not be in any sense a whitewashing committee but will deal thoroughly with Canada's war effort. I hope it will consider the whole war effort, not from any partisan point of view but for the purpose of letting the people know the real facts with regard to what Canada is doing, and be in effect a fact-finding committee. If the committee is intended to be a business committee, appointed to go over all exjtenditures incurred since the war-expenditures past and current- in connection with defence and all that sort of thing, very well and good. But I hope that the committee when appointed will cover all the ground and will see to it that the Canadian people are given the real facts about our war effort-
And value for their money. I may say that that was not carried out. What was done at almost the first meeting of the- committee? They passed a resolution to the effect that they had nothing to do with past expenditures on the war, and that they were only conducting a post mortem and decided on a whitewash of the war money spent. That is all this committee is doing; it is just conducting a post mortem over expenditures, and it sits mostly and almost entirely when the house is not sitting, and meet as various subcommittees to find out nothing, owing to the text of the resolution.
The committee of this parliament operates in an altogether different fashion from the

TFar Expenditures-Mr. Church
committee in England. I hold in my hand the last report 'of the war expenditures committee to the house, and I can say that the house has not yet seen it, and the house has been refused the right to deal with concurrence in this report. In the old country, almost every day the house meets, fifteen to twenty pages of questions on the orders of the day are asked about war expenditures, and it saves extended debates such as this. On the other hand, we in this parliament who are proceeding to spend billions of dollars are doing so without any control over the executive.
On November 3, 1941, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked if it was the intention of the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) to move concurrence in interim reports 4, 5, 6 and 7 of the special committee on war expenditures, which had been tabled that day. The Minister of National War Services who, I believe, was chairman of the committee, said that he did not think there was any intention of doing so. Following that, the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) asked if an opportunity would be given to discuss the report. To this hour no discussion has yet been held.
What is the object of the committee, if the house is to have no control over it or deal with its findings? Here we are, spending these large sums of money. As we go about the country we see lots of waste. I could take any hon. member right to Toronto, and I could show him around the normal school where there has been a great waste of public money in connection with the erection of buildings at that point, when the government could have obtained other buildings, possibly at no expense of public property and schools, for the same purpose. Just look out of a train window when passing along the Toronto waterfront, and one will see the numerous huts built along there. Many of them are vacant. I am not attempting to criticize the three war ministers-far from it. But it was stated by one minister in the house at the last session that those ministers had not located the various camps from Vancouver to Halifax, but that they had been located by the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I can tell the house that after some of those camps were established it was most difficult to get sewers, water supply and transportation facilities, and in the winter weather get proper training.
Then, let us consider the purchase of ships. What information can we get about them or about those sold before the war for a trifle? The history with respect to select committees
has always been the same. The standing committees are all right, because they stick to their task. It is altogether different, however, in regard to select committees. I have been in the house since 1921, and I have never known a select committee to do anything useful. I am not making these observations in any partisan sense, but it is a fact that the party in power selects the members of a committee, and it prepares the text of the resolution appointing such committee and drafts the report to the house. These select committees are bound by the resolutions setting them up, and they must operate within the four corners of their orders of reference. They cannot go beyond those four corners.
We had a committee on Atlantic shipping. We had a committee in connection with the customs scandal. We had another committee which dealt with Beauharnois. There was another committee to consider pric.e spreads, and another to consider the Canadian National estimates and the public accounts in connection with the Bren gun. All those committees did not find a thing useful, made reports to the house, and they were discussed, except the Bren.
I am not casting reflections upon such committees, but I do know that the government has always had one or two ministers on each committee, and that majorities have always written the reports. There has always been a good deal of partisanship in the work of such committees, and that is bound to take place under this parliamentary government. It is true that the report of a select committee when presented to the house is to a great extent a partisan report, and sometimes a minority report is made also.
I understand all parties are united in the war effort, and for the remainder of the session I should like to see all other domestic discussions, except those having to do with the war, excluded. We have now reached the fifty-third day, and it is only at this time that the motion has been presented to deal with war expenditures. The committee which sat last summer did not deal with the important question of rearranging of soldiers' pay. There should be a better system of soldiers' pay, for the lower paid groups. That matter was not heard of until, after I dealt with it many times, it was discussed in the house. Then, these dollar-a-year men, and many price and trade controllers have been appointed since that committee sat, and there should be some discussion on that point, because they are a law unto themselves and spend millions over our heads as they like.

War Expenditures-Mr. Church
I notice the resolution states:
That a select committee be appointed to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein, and that notwithstanding standing order 65 the committee shall consist of twenty-four members. . . .
And then the members are listed. When the committee of last session presented its report there were no discussions in the house. No concurrence was moved in any of its work.
We are spending money like water. Large amounts of money are spent in an unknown way, and we have no control at all over expenditures when a mint of money is being spent. Since the last- committee met there have been several innovations.
We have this price ceiling board and many others which have been set up under the War Measures Act. They have roving commissions to go all over Canada and there is no control over their expenditures. Six weeks ago a motion was moved by me for particulars about the dealings of this board and corporation on ceiling subsidies, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to give any information. During the Easter recess the chairman of the board announced that the expenditures on subsidies were up to $2,000,000, and two weeks later the Minister of Finance gave out approximately the same figure. We have information with reference to victory loans and war savings certificates, and we are told that $9,000,000 was the amount of the expenses in connection with the 1941 victory loan. The details have been refused. Entertainments of various kinds have been held; many expenses have been incurred, and yet the public are denied information, although these will add to the interest to be paid on the loans. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), who was a member of the war expenditures committee, dealt with this matter on March 5, 1941, when he said, as reported on page 1267 of Hansard:
We can go back to other days. I do not use the word "whitewash" which was employed by my hon. friend (Mr. Church) a few minutes ago. It describes rather well, however, what happened in the days of the customs investigation, what happened in the price spreads investigation, yes, and what has happened in every committee that has sat on any special problem in the last twenty years to my own knowledge.
These outside boards have been spending money like water. Last session I asked the Prime Minister what the other legislative body that meets in another place in this building was doing and if he would give them useful
[Mr. Church.)
work to do. They have met for about six hours since last June. Why should their services not be utilized? They have a number of financial men and able parliamentarians there whose services could be used to advantage in doing some of this work in such a war crisis as this. Why are they not summoned and given some of this war work to do? They might be asked to do this work, even though it meant that they had to meet every day. The system is all wrong and it cannot go on much longer. The country is heading for bankruptcy unless we protect the business man and the taxpayer. Too much money is now being taken from him. The small business man has been put out of business. Without any authority from this parliament the small retail business man in Toronto and other cities has had so many artificial burdens, barriers and restraints of trade placed on him in connection with the conduct of his business that he is losing his business and the right to make a living. We are sitting here as a parliament; yet we do nothing about it, and this is the fifty-third day of the session. The whole system is wrong and it must be changed. Parliament must regain control over the expenditures of these bodies. It is now or never. If we do not do so, then parliament might just as well be abolished. We may as well go home and leave the conduct of business to the executive. No matter what motion is proposed, objection is raised by the Minister of Finance.
With all due respect to the present Minister of Finance and without intending any disparagement whatever of him, I must say that he has not had the necessary financial training or experience for this important position in times like these and relies on men who are not experts in finance. A total of $2,200,000,000 may be spent over parliament's head for next year, without any adequate control. They would not allow that in England or in Washington. As a member of the House of Commons I wish to protest against these outlandish expenditures being made without any control by this house.

I rise to a point of order. When the house adjourned last evening the minister who was leading the house made the distinct statement that to-morrow we would continue with the present discussion, which had to do with the resolution for $2,000,000,000. When we met to-day the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) moved this motion to set up this committee, and a debate has developed, unexpectedly to me.
Mr, RALSTON: And to me.

War Expenditures-Mr. Blackmore

The effect has been to prevent us from reaching the orders of the day, for which hon. members have been waiting all afternoon. I suggest to the Prime Minister that someone move the adjournment of this debate just before six o'clock so that we can have the orders of the day called. I think that is only fair in view of what occurred last night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it is understood that the references that are made to the matters to be taken up for consideration relate to those items which stand on the order paper as government orders. It is always understood that a preliminary motion is liable to be discussed, unless there is some special question raised about it. I do not think there are many who still desire to continue the discussion this afternoon, and I should think that it still may be possible to give an opportunity to any hon. member who wishes to ask a question on the orders of the day to do so before we adjourn. I would be the last speaker on the motion, and I promise to make my remarks exceedingly brief. I think we ought to continue.

I have been impressed more or less with the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). I was not a member of the committee which sat last year, but I was in close contact with its activities through our own members. I believe that altogether too little time is being allowed1 for so extensive a task as is assigned to this committee by the resolution. I should like to divide what it is proposed that it shall do. First, this committee is to examine the expenditures defrayed out of money provided by parliament for the defence services. Second, "and for other services directly connected with the war." That could cover the raising of wheat, the production of honey, the production of wool, and so on. Third, "and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein."
I agree entirely with the purpose of the committee as set forth in this resolution, but to expect hon. members to accept in sincerity that as being the real purpose of this committee is to execute a farce. This committee has only twenty-four members, and even though it sat every day from now to the end of the year it would have no chance whatsoever of accomplishing any one of these three tasks, let alone all three. I do not wish to be merely critical. I aim not to speak any more in this house than I feel it
my duty to do. There are members who talk about the amount of time that wre spend talking, but I should like to ask any one of those members who spoke a few moments ago what on earth else they think a member of parliament can do in this house except talk? What is he sent here for if it is not to talk? There is an attitude developing in the minds of members and some people throughout the country, and in certain newspapers, which is altogether subversive to democratic government. I am not in favour of wasting the time of the house or of spending it in unnecessary discussion, but there is business for the members of this house to do. How on earth they can go through a time like this, travelling uncharted ways, without spending time in discussing matters, I should like to have the Toronto Telegram and three or four more Canadian newspapers tell me.

Leave the Telegram
alone.
Name any one of them, I do not care which; most of them are tarred with the same brush.
The Evening Telegram is a great supporter of the working man.

Then let us support the Evening Telegram. I have three or four suggestions which may be of value in connection with the work of the war expenditures committee. Could the Prime Minister not arrange it so that the committee would have power to add to its numbers indefinitely? That has not been provided for here. Can not the Prime Minister say to the committee: "Look here, this job we are giving you to do is no joke. We want you to understand you must do this job and do it right, and then come back here and report to this house in a manner that will not only satisfy the house but the country. We will give you all the facilities that will enable you to do that, not only in the amount of time at your disposal, but in the number of members you shall have power to appoint."
I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Broadview was a good one, that the services of the members of the other house should be used. I do not know what on earth this country is paying the members of the other house $4,000 a year for, if it is not to come here and do something; and why in the world they should not in these times participate in the work of this committee is beyond me. They will have to explain why in order to satisfy me.

War Expenditures-Mr. Blackmore
Why should the war expenditures committee not have power to add to its numbers indefinitely, from the members not only of this house but of the other house; and if the membership is still thought inadequate, why not bring in public-spirited men from the outside who are prepared to cooperate with the committee?
I must confess that no one, no matter what his previous business may be, can come in here and undertake to deal with the tremendous affairs of a country like this in a time like this without being bewildered by his own inability to comprehend the hugeness of the whole thing, be he as earnest and sincere as he may, and no party in this house lacks either earnestness or sincerity in dealing with the conditions we are facing to-day. Nevertheless we must have some facilities through which to work. Why not let the war expenditures committee be one of these facilities?
Having given the committee power to add to its numbers, the Prime Minister should then say to them: "You are free to sit whenever you like." It will be argued that this would cost a great deal of money, but I do not think any business concern ever lost money by paying it out for adequate supervision, and I do not think this country will lose money by paying it out for adequate supervision of its affairs in these times.
The details of the task of the committee suggest another thought to me. It will be noticed that the committee is to consider contracts which have been awarded. I am really surprised to hear that the contracts let under the Department of Munitions and Supply were not brought under review by the committee of last year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend has not been in the house. All that was explained a short time ago. The contracts were under review when the committee met last year. There is no limitation in that respect.
We did not reach them.

I beg pardon for bringing up that point on which I should have been better informed, but I was unavoidably out of the house when that explanation was made. I had understood that the committee did not reach those contracts last year.
There were many sessions of the committee devoted to munitions and supply.
When?
Right at the commencement.
Not to my knowledge.
The hon. member was not on the committee at that time.

I am glad to hear
that the committee was more effective than I had been led to believe, but let us hope that it goes even more fully into these matters in future. All one has to do is to look at these thick blue-backed books which are coming to us from time to time, listing the contracts which have been let under the Department of Munitions and Supply, to know that about all the supervision that the committee was able to give to those contracts was what we give to estimates that are being considered in the very hot weather after midnight when we s'ometimes pass millions of estimates with a wave of the hand. I do not think that is good enough; I should like to see the committee go into these contracts with much greater care.
There is another thing with which I believe the committee should deal. Since arriving in Ottawa in the winter I have had come to my desk about twenty letters, speaking from memory, from various parts of Canada. They are more or less confidential letters, telling me about waste, inefficiency and irregularities in various war activities. I would not blame the government for this at all. I have not risen and said anything on the floor of the house about these complaints. In many instances I have not even spoken to the minister about them, which would be the first thing I would do, for the simple reason that I realize that under the circumstances the minister cannot possibly take care of such matters. But why should not this committee as a part of its work investigate these complaints which are brought to the attention of members of the house? Some of the complaints are very bad; I am sure that if the Prime Minister heard about them, he would have more difficulty in resting at night. But he is not to blame, nor is the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). The work is so big and the means of control are so meagre, that these things cannot be avoided until they are brought to one's attention. There must be a way of getting around the difficulty. I would suggest that one way is to let the committee consider the complaints which come in to the members of the house, and which they could present to the committee either by word of mouth or by means of the letters.

Privilege-Mr. Pouliot
